title: This they call yoga
theme: That firm holding of the senses they consider yoga; then one becomes heedful, for yoga comes and goes.

words.role: object of manyante; refers back to the state of 2.3.10
predicate of tām, marked by iti
marks yogam as what it is called

sandhi.type: m before a consonant; m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः). Final m stays before a vowel and is joined to it.

Visarga before t becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).
-aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

morphology.note: A dvandva in the dual, set as predicate to the singular yogaḥ: ‘yoga is arising-and-passing-away’, that is, it has both. Śaṅkara takes it so, «उपजनापायधर्मक इत्यर्थः»; Raṅgarāmānuja gives that sense and a second, ‘the means of bringing about what is wanted and removing what is unwanted’ (see the commentary).
a- + pramatta, past participle of pra + √mad, ‘careless, distracted’: ‘not careless’.

translation.literal: That they consider yoga — the firm holding of the senses. Heedful then one becomes; for yoga [is] arising and passing away.
translation.readable: This steady holding of the senses is what they call yoga. At that time one must be watchful, for yoga comes and goes.

syntax: tām (the state of 2.3.10) is the object of manyante with yogam iti as its predicate; sthirām indriyadhāraṇām stands in apposition to tām. The second line has a short clause with the subject understood (apramattas tadā bhavati) and a verbless reason clause, yogo hi prabhavāpyayau.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: when the intellect has stopped there is no room for carelessness, so the heedfulness is enjoined for the time before, «तस्मात्प्रागेव बुद्ध्यादिचेष्टोपरमात् अप्रमादो विधीयते»; or else, once the holding of the senses is firm, heedfulness is unhindered. Raṅgarāmānuja: attentiveness comes when the senses stop working, «इन्द्रियाणां निर्व्यापारत्वे एव अवहितचित्तता भवति».

Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja: yoga arises and perishes, so watchfulness is needed, «योगस्य प्रतिक्षणापायशालितया अवधानम् अपेक्षितमिति भावः» (Raṅgarāmānuja). Raṅgarāmānuja also gives a second reading: yoga is the means to every human aim, bringing what is wanted and removing what is not, «इष्टप्रभवानिष्टाप्ययलक्षणसर्वपुरुषार्थसाधनत्वात् योगस्य». Madhva reads the arising and passing away as coming from the Lord (see the commentary).

metre.name: irregular
metre.note: Counted as written, 16 and 17 syllables. The first line is a regular anuṣṭubh line (8 + 8). In the second, apramattas tadā bhavati has nine syllables; yogo hi prabhavāpyayau has eight.

beginner: The previous verse described the senses, mind and intellect all coming to rest. Here that state gets its name: yoga, the steady holding of the senses. The verse then gives a warning. At such a time one must be watchful, because yoga ‘comes and goes’: a state that arises can also slip away. Śaṅkara points out that people call it yoga, joining, though it is really a separation from everything that brings harm. He adds that the watchfulness has to be practised beforehand, since once the mind is fully still there is no room left for carelessness. Raṅgarāmānuja gives the same warning and a second reading of the last words: yoga is the means of gaining what is good and removing what is bad. Madhva reads the arising and passing away as coming from the Lord.
analogy: Holding a full cup steady is easy for a moment; the skill is not letting it tip when your attention wanders.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The steady holding of the senses is called yoga; then one must be heedful, for yoga arises and passes away.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: a joining that is a separation
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: They call it yoga though it is really disjunction, «योगमिति मन्यन्ते वियोगमेव सन्तम्»: this state of the yogin is marked by separation from union with every harm, «सर्वानर्थसंयोगवियोगलक्षणा हीयमवस्था योगिनः». Heedful means free from carelessness and always making effort towards composure, «प्रमादवर्जितः समाधानं प्रति नित्यं यत्नवान्». Yoga has arising and passing away, «उपजनापायधर्मक इत्यर्थः», so heedfulness must guard against its loss, «अतः अपायपरिहारायाप्रमादः कर्तव्य इत्यभिप्रायः».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: a highest course that must be guarded
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The holding of the outer and inner faculties named in the last verse is called yoga, and he quotes Vyāsārya: «परमागतिर्योग». Yoga can lapse at any moment, so attention is needed, «योगस्य प्रतिक्षणापायशालितया अवधानम् अपेक्षितमिति भावः»; or, since yoga is the means to every aim, «इष्टप्रभवानिष्टाप्ययलक्षणसर्वपुरुषार्थसाधनत्वात् योगस्य», one must be heedful in it.

commentary.q: Madhva: arising and passing away from the Lord
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: He glosses the last words: yoga is towards arising and passing away, «प्रभवाप्ययौ प्रति हि योगः», and these come from the Lord, «भगवतस्सकाशात् प्रभवाप्ययौ».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara’s phrase, a ‘joining’ that is a separation from harm, matches the Gītā’s definition of yoga as disjunction from union with sorrow: «तं विद्याद्दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसञ्ज्ञितम्».

advaita.text: Yoga is separation from every harm, «सर्वानर्थसंयोगवियोगलक्षणा हीयमवस्था योगिनः»; because it can be lost, heedfulness must be practised.

visistadvaita.text: Yoga is the highest course and the means to every human aim, and must be guarded because it can lapse at any moment, «योगस्य प्रतिक्षणापायशालितया अवधानम् अपेक्षितमिति भावः».

dvaita.text: The arising and passing away the verse speaks of come from the Lord, «भगवतस्सकाशात् प्रभवाप्ययौ».

schools.disagreement: Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja read prabhavāpyayau of yoga itself, which comes and goes; Raṅgarāmānuja adds that it brings what is good and removes what is bad. Madhva’s short gloss ties the arising and passing away to the Lord.

parallels.note: The Gītā’s definition of yoga as disjunction from sorrow.
The tortoise drawing in its limbs: the senses withdrawn from their objects.

parallels.quote: अध्यात्मयोगाधिगमेन देवं मत्वा धीरो हर्षशोकौ जहाति
parallels.note: The Kaṭha’s first mention of yoga, the inward yoga by which the god in the cave is known.

contemporary.text: Any discipline that is hard to reach is easy to lose. The verse names the stillness of the senses and in the same breath warns that it does not stay by itself. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What good habit of yours comes and goes, and what keeps it?
reflect.deeper: Śaṅkara calls yoga a ‘separation’. From what, and why might the word still be ‘joining’?
reflect.practice: When a moment of quiet comes, notice what is most likely to end it.

flags.note: prabhavāpyayau of yoga itself, which arises and passes (Śaṅkara, Raṅgarāmānuja), with Raṅgarāmānuja’s second reading (the means of gaining the good and removing the bad), and Madhva’s gloss tying arising and passing away to the Lord.
madhva.json files Madhva’s line on yogo hi prabhavāpyayau (॥ ९-११ ॥) under both 2.3.10 and 2.3.11; it concerns this mantra only.
